water.name: Water
water.description: The universal solvent essential for all known forms of life.
funFacts: Water is the only natural substance that exists in all three physical states at temperatures normally found on Earth.
A water molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about 9 days before falling as precipitation.
Hot water can freeze faster than cold water — this is known as the Mpemba effect.

methane.name: Methane
methane.description: The simplest hydrocarbon and a potent greenhouse gas.
uses: Natural gas fuel for heating and cooking
funFacts: Methane is 80× more potent than CO₂ as a greenhouse gas over a 20-year period.
Its perfect tetrahedral shape gives all four C–H bonds equal length (1.09 Å).
Methanogenic archaea produce methane deep in ocean sediments and cow digestive systems.

glucose.name: Glucose
glucose.description: Primary energy source for cells and a fundamental sugar in biology.
uses: Primary cellular energy source via glycolysis
IV glucose drips in medical care
Fermentation to produce ethanol and CO₂
funFacts: Your brain consumes about 120g of glucose per day — roughly 60% of your total glucose usage.
Glucose exists in two forms: α-glucose and β-glucose, which differ only in the orientation of one hydroxyl group.
A single gram of glucose releases approximately 4 Calories when metabolized.

caffeine.name: Caffeine
caffeine.description: A central nervous system stimulant found in coffee and tea.
uses: Stimulant in coffee, tea, and energy drinks
Treatment of apnea in premature infants
funFacts: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors in the brain, preventing the feeling of tiredness.
The average cup of espresso contains about 63mg of caffeine — a lethal dose would require ~80 cups consumed very rapidly.
Caffeine is the world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance.

dna-fragment.name: DNA Base Pair
dna-fragment.description: A hydrogen-bonded base pair forming the rungs of the DNA double helix.
uses: Genetic information storage in all living organisms
funFacts: Adenine always pairs with Thymine via 2 hydrogen bonds — this is Watson-Crick base pairing.
If the DNA from all your cells were uncoiled and laid end-to-end, it would reach from Earth to the Sun and back ~600 times.
The human genome contains approximately 3 billion base pairs.

protein-fragment.name: Peptide Bond
protein-fragment.description: A dipeptide fragment showing the fundamental peptide bond linkage.
uses: Fundamental unit of all protein structures
Template for synthetic peptide drug design
Food flavoring agents (e.g., aspartame is a dipeptide)
funFacts: The peptide bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance — it's planar and doesn't freely rotate.
There are 20 standard amino acids, and life uses combinations of them to build over 100,000 distinct human proteins.
The ribosome synthesizes a new peptide bond roughly every 0.05 seconds.

ethanol.name: Ethanol
ethanol.description: The familiar two-carbon alcohol behind beer, wine, and antiseptic gels—small, polar, and surprisingly influential in chemistry labs and parties alike.
funFacts: Your liver turns ethanol into acetaldehyde before it becomes acetate—pace matters.
Ethanol disrupts membrane fluidity and protein structure, which is part of why it's such a broad biological solvent.

aspirin.name: Aspirin
aspirin.description: Acetylsalicylic acid: a classic pain reliever that irreversibly tweaks platelet chemistry—medicine, history, and organic synthesis in one tiny tablet.
funFacts: Willow bark salicin is the plant-world ancestor of this synthetic superstar.
Its acetyl group helps it survive stomach acid better than salicylic acid alone.

capsaicin.name: Capsaicin
capsaicin.description: The fiery vanilloid that makes chili peppers bite—an evolutionary deterrent for mammals and a neuroscientist's favorite TRPV1 conversation starter.
funFacts: Birds often lack the receptor sensitivity mammals have—chili seeds spread farther that way.
Spice "heat" is not a taste on the tongue map; it's nociceptor theater.

serotonin.name: Serotonin
serotonin.description: 5-HT: a monoamine signal with a résumé spanning mood, sleep, and gut motility—proof that one scaffold can wear many biological hats.
uses: Pharmacology targets (e.g. SSRIs act upstream in pathways)
Peripheral roles in the enteric nervous system
funFacts: Most of your body's serotonin isn't "in your mood"—a large share is entangled with the gut and platelets.
Its name nods to blood serum, where it was first noticed to constrict vessels.

dopamine.name: Dopamine
dopamine.description: A catecholamine built from a brave little ethylamine tail on a catechol ring—motivation, movement, and mesolimbic myths all orbit this structure.
uses: Neurotransmitter in reward and motor pathways
Clinical shock support (as hydrochloride salt, IV, under care)
Teaching ligand for GPCR and transporter biology
funFacts: Parkinson's pathology is tightly linked to dopamine neuron loss in the substantia nigra.
It's polar enough that free dopamine doesn't casually joyride across the blood–brain barrier.

adrenaline.name: Adrenaline
adrenaline.description: Epinephrine: the molecule behind the pulse spike when something jumps in the bushes—sympathetic chemistry distilled into three oxygens of urgency.
funFacts: "Adrenaline" vs "epinephrine" is largely UK/US naming—they're the same impatient little hormone.
It hits α- and β-adrenergic receptors, explaining both vasoconstriction stories and bronchodilator uses.

buckminsterfullerene.name: Buckminsterfullerene
buckminsterfullerene.description: Soccer-ball symmetry in pure carbon—a Nobel-celebrated cage that taught us aromaticity doesn't require flat hexagons.
bondTypes: Delocalized π systems on curved surfaces
uses: Electron acceptor motifs in organic electronics research
funFacts: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons—Euler's handshake with graphite's wild cousin.
Named after architect Buckminster Fuller, who popularized geodesic domes.

heme-group.name: Hemoglobin Heme Group
heme-group.description: The iron-chelating porphyrin prosthetic group that turns hemoglobin into an oxygen shuttle: reversible O₂ binding with protein allostery backstage.
uses: O₂ transport and storage inside hemoproteins
Biochemistry teaching for ligand-field and cooperative binding
funFacts: Four heme units in hemoglobin enable cooperative binding—sigmoidal curves aren't chemistry trivia, they're physiology.
The axial histidine tug-of-war fine-tunes oxygen affinity versus CO competition.

methane-combustion.name: Combustion of Methane
methane-combustion.description: A classic oxidation: methane meets oxygen in a chain of radical steps that release a lot of heat and produce carbon dioxide and water.

quickFacts.summary: Complete combustion of methane is strongly exothermic and converts chemical potential energy into heat and light.
quickFacts.energyProfile: Highly exothermic (ΔH << 0 for the balanced reaction)
quickFacts.mechanism: Radical chain mechanism: initiation → propagation (·OH, ·CH₃, etc.) → termination; 3D view highlights representative species.
quickFacts.highlight: Every balanced combustion story ends with better CO₂ accounting and careful handling of open flames.

water-formation.name: Formation of Water
water-formation.description: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to make water — simple stoichiometry, enormous industrial and rocket-science relevance.

quickFacts.summary: This reaction releases a large amount of energy per gram of H₂, which is why it powers clean-energy conversations.
quickFacts.conditions: Ignition or catalyst (e.g. Pt); precise H₂ : O₂ ratio matters for safety
quickFacts.mechanism: Often radical-mediated in the gas phase; the 3D view shows the polar product that emerges from redox partnership.
quickFacts.highlight: The bent geometry of water is a direct consequence of lone-pair repulsion on oxygen.

glucose-fermentation.name: Fermentation of Glucose
glucose-fermentation.description: Yeast-friendly biochemistry: glucose is split into ethanol and carbon dioxide — the reason bread rises and wine exists.

quickFacts.summary: Glycolysis followed by fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep running when oxygen is scarce.
quickFacts.energyProfile: Partial oxidation — modest ATP compared to respiration
quickFacts.conditions: Yeast or bacteria; anaerobic or microaerobic environment
quickFacts.mechanism: Pyruvate → acetaldehyde → ethanol, with CO₂ lost as a small molecule.
quickFacts.highlight: The same pathway family connects brewing, baking, and biofuel research.

haber-bosch.name: Haber-Bosch Process
haber-bosch.description: Industrial nitrogen fixation: atmospheric N₂ and H₂ are converted to ammonia—the backbone of global fertilizer production.

quickFacts.summary: The industrial implementation of nitrogen fixation, transforming atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia to produce fertilizers that sustain global food production.
quickFacts.conditions: High pressure (150–250 bar), high temperature (400–500°C), and an iron (Fe) catalyst.
quickFacts.mechanism: Dissociative adsorption of N₂ and H₂ gases on the iron catalyst surface, followed by stepwise hydrogenation of nitrogen atoms.

photosynthesis.name: Photosynthesis (Simplified)
photosynthesis.description: Light-driven carbon fixation: six CO₂ and six water molecules are built into one glucose ring while releasing oxygen—the metabolic engine of the biosphere.

quickFacts.summary: The foundational biochemical process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose), releasing oxygen as a byproduct.
quickFacts.energyProfile: Endothermic / Endergonic (requires photon energy, ΔH = +2803 kJ/mol for the overall simplified equation).
quickFacts.mechanism: Light-dependent reactions split water to generate ATP and NADPH, followed by the light-independent Calvin Cycle fixing CO₂ into a 6-carbon sugar.

neutralization-hcl-naoh.name: Neutralization (HCl + NaOH)
neutralization-hcl-naoh.description: A textbook Arrhenius neutralization: strong acid and strong base form a salt and water—the proton-transfer reaction every intro chemistry student meets first.

quickFacts.summary: A classic Arrhenius acid-base reaction where a strong acid and a strong base neutralize each other to produce a salt (sodium chloride) and water.
quickFacts.mechanism: Proton transfer where H⁺ ions from the acid combine with OH⁻ ions from the base to form stable covalent H₂O molecules, while Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain as spectator ions or form a crystalline lattice upon evaporation.

esterification-ethyl-acetate.name: Esterification (Ethyl Acetate)
esterification-ethyl-acetate.description: Fischer esterification: carboxylic acid and alcohol condense into a fruity ester plus water—equilibrium chemistry with a touch of sulfuric acid and heat.

quickFacts.summary: A condensation reaction between an organic acid (acetic acid) and an alcohol (ethanol) to produce an ester (ethyl acetate, known for its sweet, fruity odor) and water.
quickFacts.conditions: Acid catalyst (typically concentrated H₂SO₄) and heat under reflux.
quickFacts.mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution. The carbonyl oxygen of the carboxylic acid is protonated, followed by a nucleophilic attack by the alcohol's hydroxyl group, culminating in the elimination of a water molecule.
